questions.q: What is a Key Vault "secret" used for?
options: Only storing encryption keys used for encryption at rest
Storing arbitrary sensitive strings like a connection string, API key, or storage access key
Storing Azure Active Directory user passwords for sign-in
Only storing TLS/SSL certificates
questions.explain: Secrets are a separate Key Vault object type from certificates and encryption keys -- they hold small sensitive strings like connection strings and API keys.

questions.q: How does an Azure resource with a Managed Identity retrieve a Key Vault secret?
options: It emails the vault administrator to request the value manually
It requests a token from Azure AD proving its identity, then presents that token to Key Vault instead of storing a credential itself
It stores the vault's master password in its own configuration file
It hardcodes the secret once and caches it permanently
questions.explain: Managed Identity lets Azure manage the resource's identity automatically, so the app authenticates with a token rather than a stored password or certificate.

questions.q: What decides which identities are allowed to read a given secret in Key Vault?
options: Only the original creator of the vault can ever read any secret
Any identity in the same Azure subscription can read any secret by default
Access policies, or the newer Azure RBAC model, configured by the vault owner
Secrets in Key Vault have no access control once they are stored
questions.explain: Access policies (or RBAC roles like Key Vault Secrets User) explicitly grant get/list rights -- everything else is denied by default.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the real security boundary is the access policy, not the fact that a value is 'in Key Vault'?
options: Key Vault secrets cannot be read by any identity, even authorized ones
Key Vault automatically encrypts secrets so access control is unnecessary
Storing a secret safely doesn't matter if every identity in the subscription can still read it
Access policies are optional and rarely configured in practice
questions.explain: A typical setup grants read access only to the one managed identity that needs a specific secret, denying every other identity by default -- that's what actually limits exposure.

questions.q: In the lesson's pseudocode example, why does the application code contain no password?
options: It uses DefaultAzureCredential backed by a managed identity to authenticate, then calls get_secret() to retrieve the value at runtime
The example intentionally omits the password for brevity, but a real version needs one
Key Vault requires no authentication at all to retrieve a secret
The password is stored in an environment variable in plain text instead
questions.explain: The managed identity provides authentication to Key Vault, so the actual secret value is only ever retrieved into memory at runtime -- never written into the code.
